titulo.texto: Models of Houses and Scenes from Nayarit and Jalisco

frase_gancho.texto: Little clay houses with banquets and dogs: the world of the living, in miniature.

puente_narrativo.texto: From houses we move on to animals. Look for a red clay vessel, polished and shiny, shaped like a bird with a curved beak, like a parrot.

guion_corto.texto: These clay models come from the Shaft Tombs of Nayarit and Jalisco and were made about two thousand years ago. They are miniature houses, with steeply sloped thatched roofs painted with geometric designs, and tiny figures inside or in front of them. Other models show scenes with many figures, such as gatherings, rituals, and even a ball game. In some houses there are two levels: upstairs a banquet seems to be taking place, and downstairs someone is grinding maize, with a dog at the door. They look like an ordinary day, but they were made for a tomb. It is thought that they recreate the world of the living so that the dead person could take it along. Today they are one of the few windows onto those houses, because the real ones, made of fragile materials, have vanished.

guion_largo.texto:
What was a house in western Mexico like two thousand years ago? Hardly any houses remain to answer that. They were built with poles, mud, and straw, and time carried them away. Of many, only oval mounds of earth survive, where the foundations once stood. That is why these models are so valuable: in them, the house is still standing.

The potters of the Ixtlán del Río style, in Nayarit, modeled them with great care. The thatched roof is steeply sloped and carries painted geometric designs. There are red and black diamonds nested one inside another, and bands of triangles. The designs run down the walls to the base. In front there are clay people, and sometimes another peeks out from inside. The ones known measure between twenty-five and thirty-six centimeters tall, about what fits between your hands. These people have simple faces, with large heads and prominent noses, almost like caricatures. But their gestures suggest conversation and shared food.

One of the most complete, now kept in a museum in New York, has two floors. Upstairs there is a banquet: adults seated before the food, a pregnant woman leaning on a post, and a man with a large necklace at the top of the stairs. Downstairs, a woman grinds maize on the metate, the grinding stone, and two other people prepare a dish to carry up. At the entrance, a dog waits.

This is not the portrait of an ordinary day. At that time, people were sometimes buried beneath their own homes. Some models have openings in the base that suggest a tomb shaft. A specialist, Kristi Butterwick, proposes that the room below represents the tomb and that above, a gathering is being held for the death. It could also simply be a kitchen. It has also been proposed that it recalls an important event, such as the death of a leading figure or the naming of a new chief.

One idea sums up many readings: these models rebuild the world of the living to create one for the dead. The [shaft tomb you saw](mna_s10_tumba_tiro) did the very same thing, with its vessels and its figures. Even the dog at the door has its reason: dogs and birds were food, and dogs were believed to guide the dead, like those of Colima.

The MNA holds models of this kind. In a house from Nayarit, about thirty centimeters tall, all the figures are men. That is why it is thought not to be a family gathering, but a formal meeting or a ritual in which food is shared.

Not all of them are houses. Others are public scenes with many figures. One of them is a ball court, with spectators above and players below. One of the players strikes the ball with his knee. It is the same game you saw at the [marker from Chinkultic](mna_s09_disco_chinkultic). Scenes with dozens of figures are concentrated in Nayarit and Jalisco.

Almost all of these pieces came from looting. Archaeologists did not find an intact shaft tomb until 1993, in Huitzilapa, Jalisco. That is why we know so little about the tomb of each model. Even so, look at what they tell: people eating, talking, waiting. It is the life of a village that left no writing, told in clay.

texto: Look for the thatched roof and the geometric designs painted on it
Count the tiny figures and notice what they seem to be doing
See whether there is a dog, a bird, or another animal in the scene

texto.Period: Late Preclassic to Early Classic (around 300 BC-300 AD)
texto.Material: Modeled ceramic with slip and paint
texto.Origin: Shaft Tombs of Nayarit (Ixtlán del Río style) and Jalisco
texto.Dimensions: the known houses measure between 25 and 36 cm tall

texto.pregunta: Myth: These little houses simply show an ordinary day in the village.
texto.respuesta: Reality: They were made for a tomb. Specialists think they recreate the world of the living for the deceased, with banquets, rituals, and important gatherings.
